problems.source_says: No participant used an AI tool at any point. The paper describes the ChatGPT-labeled list as a step before the DAT: participants saw the list, retyped it, rated it, and then 'Lastly' completed the DAT 'themselves'. Section 3.1 says participants rated the prime 'before completing the Divergent Association Task', and Figure 1 draws Prime, Perceived Prime Creativity, and DAT as successive boxes. The DAT rules tell participants to 'Think of the words on your own'. The paper never says the list stayed on screen during the DAT. So the text gives no support for 'yes', and it leans toward 'no'. The form's own reconciliation lists this field as 'Kept as yes, not confirmed'. Reconciled c158 S1-O14 codes a DAT that participants took alone right after the AI step as 'no'.
problems.quote: To ensure that the participants had read this prime, they were asked to retype the list of words presented. Participants were then asked, “how creative do you think this list is?” Lastly, participants completed the DAT themselves.
problems.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2 and Figure 1; p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 5, Section 3.5.2.2, DAT rule 5; c097 form, reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked (confirmed: false); forms/c158.json S1-O14

problems.source_says: with_ai needs AI to be available while the DAT was written, and the text does not show that (see the row above). The codebook rule says 'An outcome produced after AI is removed is after_ai whatever its construct.' On the procedure the paper describes, that rule gives after_ai, which is how reconciled c158 S1-O14 codes a DAT taken alone after the AI step. The fit is not clean. The 'AI use' here was retyping and rating one seven-word list labeled ChatGPT, and the codebook frames after_ai as work done 'after a period of AI use'. The only support for with_ai is that the paper calls the prime 'assistance given' (Hypothesis 1, p. 3). Review 1 should choose between after_ai and with_ai. The form records with_ai as if it were settled.
problems.quote: Think of the words on your own (e.g., do not just look at objects in your surroundings).

problems.source_says: The DAT asks each participant for 10 words that differ as much as possible, and the paper names its scoring method as semantic distance. The score measures how far apart one person's own words are. The codebook says 'Variety among one person's own ideas is flexibility', and it defines overall_creativity as a score of 'creativity as a whole'. The paper itself says divergent thinking 'represents only one facet of creativity' (p. 8, Section 6.1). Other reconciled forms code this same DAT score as flexibility (c126 S1-O3) or other (c069 S1-O3, c158 S1-O14). None uses overall_creativity. The form's notes name novelty as the only alternative. Flexibility fits the codebook rule better. The codebook defines flexibility as a count of categories, so Review 1 should set one DAT code for all forms.
problems.quote: Please enter 10 words that are as different from each other as possible, in all meanings and uses of the words.
problems.locator: p. 5, Section 3.5.2.2 (instructions and 'the same underlying method (semantic distance)'); p. 8, Section 6.1; codebook section 6, Construct; forms/c126.json S1-O3, forms/c069.json S1-O3, forms/c158.json S1-O14

problems.source_says: No pair of arms has its own test statistic. The only DAT statistic across arms is the six-group omnibus F (5, 375) = 6.39, which tests no single pair. The Tukey HSD result appears only in words (ChLo 'was significantly different from all other conditions'), and the Discussion calls the other conditions 'statistically indistinguishable'. No pairwise t, q, or p-value is printed. The ns are allocation counts from Table 1. Per-arm analyzed ns are not printed (381 DAT scores from 387 allocated). Each 'reported' field states these limits correctly, but the tag test_statistic suggests a pair-level test that does not exist.
problems.quote: Post hoc comparisons using the Tukey HSD test indicated that the mean DAT score for the group ChLo (M = 76.37, SD = 5.71) was significantly different from all other conditions
problems.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 7, Discussion; p. 4, Table 1; p. 5, Table 3

confirmed.statement: Criterion 3 holds. The DAT score is computed on each participant's own word list ('participants completed the DAT themselves'), and the paper names the DAT's method as semantic distance. No rater and no self-report enters the score. So scored_on_output true and measure automated_score fit, and the codebook lists 'semantic-distance scoring of divergent-thinking tests' under automated_score.

confirmed.statement: unit participant matches the paper's own analyses. A one-way between-groups ANOVA compares participants in six groups with error df 375, which fits 381 DAT scores. The hierarchical regression also has one row per participant.

confirmed.statement: All six arm means and SDs in the contrasts match the text: HuLo 79.96 (5.94), HuTy 79.74 (7.24), HuHi 82.18 (5.63), ChLo 76.37 (5.71), ChTy 81.21 (6.07), ChHi 81.11 (5.66). The points plotted in Figure 2 agree.
The omnibus test matches: F (5, 375) = 6.39, p < 0.001, eta squared = 0.08.

summary: The DAT score is a computed semantic-distance score of each participant's own word list, so criterion 3 holds, and every mean, SD, count, and test statistic in the outcome entry matches pp. 4-6 of the PDF. The coding is still refuted: no AI tool was used and participants did the DAT 'themselves' after the ChatGPT-labeled list, so ai_available_when_produced 'yes' and question with_ai lack support (the codebook rule points to after_ai), and overall_creativity departs from the codebook's flexibility rule and from how c126, c069, and c158 code the DAT.
